title: Leaving tomorrow
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on the acute medical unit. Tomorrow you start a new rotation in a different hospital. Several of your patients are still waiting for results, including a CT scan for a possible malignancy and a set of blood cultures.

The F2 who will take over your patients starts tomorrow and doesn't know them.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Ask the ward clerk to email you the results next week.
options.brief: Results should go to the doctor responsible, not to someone who has left.
options.detailed: You won't be responsible for these patients, and you won't be able to act on the results from another hospital. This creates confusion about who owns them.

options.text: Write a handover of each pending result and what to do.
options.brief: A written handover makes sure nothing is lost when you leave.
options.detailed: Results that arrive after you have gone need a clear owner and a plan. A written list, with what each result means for the patient, gives the incoming F2 everything they need. It ranks first.

options.text: Leave the results for the team to find on the computer system.
options.brief: Risks a significant result being missed.
options.detailed: A new doctor who doesn't know the patients may not know to look. A possible malignancy could be missed. It is the least appropriate option.

options.text: Tell your patients who will be looking after them from tomorrow.
options.detailed: Patients may worry when a familiar doctor leaves. Letting them know who will take over helps them feel looked after. It ranks second because it doesn't, by itself, make sure results are acted on.

options.text: Chase the results that are due today before you leave.
options.brief: Useful, but it won't capture results that come later.
options.detailed: Acting on results that arrive today reduces the load on your successor, but the CT and cultures may come later. It ranks third.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you make sure pending results have a clear owner before you leave a job.
explanation.keyDetails: Significant results are pending. Your successor doesn't know the patients. You are moving to another hospital.
explanation.reasoning: [B] gives a clear, written handover, [D] supports the patients, and [E] deals with today's results. [A] sends results to the wrong person, and [C] risks a missed diagnosis.
explanation.competing: Some would put chasing today's results second. The key ranks telling patients second because it supports their care regardless of when results arrive.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 3, handing over care safely when you change roles.
